analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from forcing workers to arbitrate discrimination claims instead of going to court.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, dying without a vote after being referred on April 13, 1994.
analysis.plain_summary: Under this bill, an employer could not make signing away your right to sue for discrimination a condition of getting or keeping a job. It would have amended the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Rehabilitation Act, and a key civil rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1981) so that firing or penalizing someone for refusing mandatory arbitration, or making arbitration a condition of employment, would itself count as unlawful discrimination.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers — especially women, older workers, people with disabilities, and workers of color — who would keep the right to take discrimination claims to court rather than being locked into private arbitration as a condition of employment, where proceedings are typically secret, use employer-selected arbitrators, and offer limited appeal.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer to fire, refuse to hire, or otherwise discriminate against a worker because the worker refuses to submit a Title VII discrimination claim to mandatory arbitration [S3].
Applies the same prohibition to age discrimination claims under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967, including federal employment [S3].

Bars employers from making arbitration a condition of hiring, continued employment, or compensation under the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (including federal employment and federal contractor employment), and Section 1981 of the Revised Statutes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who use mandatory arbitration clauses, which would lose a tool for keeping discrimination claims out of court and out of public view; arbitration firms would lose a pipeline of employment disputes if workers retained the option to sue.

drawbacks.text: The bill bars mandatory arbitration but does not prohibit voluntary arbitration after a dispute arises, so it leaves arbitration as an option while requiring employers to keep their workers' court rights intact — an approach employers argued limits the efficiency of resolving disputes outside court [S3].

Employers and arbitration providers have long contended that arbitration resolves employment disputes faster and more cheaply than litigation, and that a blanket ban removes a dispute-resolution option rather than fixing arbitration's flaws [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is large: mandatory arbitration clauses mean discrimination claims are decided in private proceedings with an arbitrator chosen under an employer's contract, no jury, limited appeal, and no public record. The main cost is to employers and the arbitration industry, and to employers' preference for cheaper, confidential dispute resolution. Whether some disputes resolve faster in arbitration is the strongest counterargument, but the bill targeted only coerced arbitration — where workers had no real choice — not voluntary agreements.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee on April 13, 1994, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Russell Feingold introduced the bill on April 13, 1994, and delivered introductory remarks in the Senate [S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S5].
No committee action, floor action, or vote followed, and the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that require workers to sign mandatory arbitration agreements, and the commercial arbitration industry, were better off because the bill died: workers remained bound to arbitrate discrimination claims under contract terms they were forced to accept. Nothing in law changed for workers during this Congress.

for.name: Sen. Russell D. Feingold
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; the bill was his response to mandatory arbitration clauses in employment contracts [S5].

for.name: 1 Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a two-senator base of support [S4].

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took it up; no markup, hearing, or vote was scheduled before the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew enough support for a partisan fight: the sponsor was a Democrat with one Democratic cosponsor, and no votes were ever recorded on it [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Mandatory arbitration clauses funnel employment discrimination disputes to private arbitrators as a condition of employment, a revenue stream this bill would have cut off. Arbitration proceedings are private, so workers lose a jury, a public record, and meaningful appeal.

The bill would have ended employers' ability to make signing away court access a condition of a job, forcing discrimination claims into a forum employers set the rules for. Employers' interest in cheaper, confidential resolution of these claims runs against workers' right to sue.
